propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of a PRRA decision dated March 23, 2015, denying the Applicant's PRRA under IRPA ss 112 and 113.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of a decision of an immigration officer (“Officer” or “PRRA Officer”) of Citizenship and Immigration Canada, dated March 23, 2015, in which the Officer denied the Applicant’s Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) pursuant to ss 112 and 113 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of a PRRA denial decision dated March 23, 2015 under IRPA ss 112 and 113.

propositions.text: Applicant is a 31-year-old Ghanaian permanent resident convicted of crimes and diagnosed with psychotic disorder and suspected schizophrenia.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a 31 year old citizen of Ghana. He came to Canada in 1998 as a permanent resident having been sponsored by his mother. In 2005, the Applicant was convicted of three criminal offences. In 2008, he was diagnosed with Psychotic Disorder Not Otherwise Specified and suspected schizophrenia (Certified Tribunal Record, p 130).

propositions.text: In 2008, IRB found Applicant criminally inadmissible and issued deportation order; appeal stayed for three years but later cancelled after reoffense.
propositions.quote: Also in 2008, the Immigration Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (“IRB”) found that the Applicant was criminally inadmissible to Canada and, on January 31, 2008, a deportation order was issued against him. The Applicant appealed the deportation order and on May 9, 2009, his removal was stayed by the Immigration Appeal Division of the IRB for three years. However, the Applicant reoffended and was convicted on May 30, 2014. On July 30, 2014, the stay of his removal was cancelled and the appeal of his January 2008 deportation order was terminated by operation of law pursuant to s 68(4) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for PRRA on Oct 21, 2014, fearing risk in Ghana due to schizophrenia; PRRA Officer denied on March 23, 2015.
propositions.quote: On October 21, 2014, the Applicant applied for a PRRA based on his belief that his life would be at risk in Ghana because he suffers from schizophrenia. On March 23, 2015, the PRRA Officer rendered a negative decision which is the subject of this application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes the Applicant's background, criminal convictions, deportation order, PRRA application, and denial.

propositions.text: PRRA Officer noted Applicant's claim of risk in Ghana due to schizophrenia and lack of family support, and counsel's submission on inadequate healthcare.
propositions.quote: In his decision, the PRRA Officer stated that the Applicant’s submissions were based on his belief that his life would be at risk in Ghana because he suffers from schizophrenia. Further, the Officer noted the Applicant’s submission that he has no immediate family in Ghana to assist him and that inadequate treatment would place him at risk of being stigmatized and/or discriminated against. He also noted counsel’s submission that Ghana’s inability to provide adequate health care would result in his illness being untreated, likely rendering the Applicant homeless.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA Officer noted the Applicant's submissions about risk from schizophrenia, lack of family support, and inadequate healthcare in Ghana.

propositions.text: PRRA Officer found insufficient evidence Applicant received medication since June 2012.
propositions.quote: The PRRA Officer found that he had been provided with insufficient objective evidence that the Applicant had seen or received medication from a doctor since June 2012.

propositions.text: Officer found discrimination against disabled persons in Ghana persists but government is making serious efforts to change this.
propositions.quote: while his independent research of country conditions clearly indicated that discrimination against persons with disabilities continues to be a problem in Ghana, it was also clear that the government was making serious efforts to change this.

propositions.text: Ghana is a democracy with functioning police and judiciary capable of assisting Applicant; thus, s 96 IRPA requirements not met.
propositions.quote: Because Ghana is a democracy with a functioning police force and a judicial system capable of assisting the Applicant should the need arise, the PRRA Officer found that the Applicant did not meet the requirements of s 96 of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Applicant not at risk of torture under s 97(1)(a) IRPA as risk arises from medical condition, not government-inflicted pain or suffering.
propositions.quote: Based on the same evidence, the PRRA Officer found that the Applicant would not be at risk of torture pursuant to s 97(1)(a) of the IRPA because the risk arose from his medical condition, it was not pain or suffering inflicted or consented to by government or its agents and therefore did not fall under the definition of torture.

propositions.text: Officer accepted 2008 diagnosis but found risk from inadequate healthcare excluded by s 97(1)(b)(iv) IRPA.
propositions.quote: The PRRA Officer accepted the 2008 diagnosis of a psychotic disorder not otherwise specified and the possibility that the Applicant’s symptoms represented the evolution of schizophrenia, but found the risk caused by Ghana’s inability to provide adequate health or medical care was excluded by s 97(1)(b)(iv) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Absence of social support in Ghana is a humanitarian factor not considered in PRRA context.
propositions.quote: Further, the absence of a social support network in Ghana was a humanitarian and compassionate factor which he was not able to consider in the context of a PRRA.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA Officer found insufficient medication evidence, noted discrimination but government efforts, found Ghana's protection adequate, and excluded risk of torture and humanitarian factors.

propositions.text: Officer found insufficient evidence of persecution on Convention grounds and unlikely risk of torture or cruel treatment on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The PRRA Officer found that there was insufficient evidence before him to conclude that the Applicant faces more than a mere possibility of persecution on any Convention ground. And, on a balance of probabilities, he found that it is not likely that the Applicant will face a risk of torture, or a risk to life or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to Ghana.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA Officer found insufficient evidence of persecution and unlikely risk of torture or cruel treatment upon return to Ghana.

propositions.text: Applicant's counsel submitted reconsideration request with doctor's note confirming recent treatment and medication.
propositions.quote: In light of the PRRA Officer’s finding that there was insufficient evidence that the Applicant was taking medication, his counsel submitted a request for reconsideration on May 15, 2015, including a doctor’s note confirming the Applicant’s recent treatment and ongoing medication.

propositions.text: Applicant claims no response to reconsideration request was received.
propositions.quote: The Applicant claims that he did not receive a response to his request.

propositions.text: Evidence submitted after decision is not part of record and not considered on judicial review (citing Assn of Universities and Colleges of Canada v Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency).
propositions.quote: However, since this letter was sent after the PRRA Officer’s decision was rendered, it was therefore not a part of the record before the PRRA Officer when he rendered his decision and, for that reason, it is also not to be considered by this Court when reviewing the Officer’s decision (Assn of Universities and Colleges of Canada v Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency, 2012 FCA 22 at paras 19-20).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submitted new medical evidence after decision; court states it cannot consider post-decision evidence on review.

propositions.text: Applicant argues PRRA Officer erred by applying 'serious efforts' test instead of operational adequacy test for state protection.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the PRRA Officer erred by applying a “serious efforts” rather than operational adequacy test when assessing whether state protection was available to him (Balogh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 76 at paras 27-28; Kanto v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 628 at para 21; Fazekas v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 694 at paras 9-11; Molnar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 296 at para 26; Gulyas v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 254 at para 79).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues the PRRA Officer wrongly applied a 'serious efforts' test instead of the operational adequacy test for state protection.

propositions.text: Applicant relied on recent HRW report showing abuses in Ghana psychiatric hospitals and prayer camps.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that in his PRRA application he had relied largely on a recent Human Rights Watch (“HRW”) report on the treatment of persons with mental health issues by psychiatric hospitals and in prayer camps in Ghana.

propositions.text: Counsel's submissions describe abuses including denial of food, medicine, overcrowding, detention, and physical/verbal abuse in prayer camps and hospitals.
propositions.quote: Those submissions by counsel state that the report discusses prayer camps run by private religious organizations where mental health patients are subjected to various abuses, including denial of food and medicine, overcrowding, prolonged detention and physical and verbal abuse. And, at Ghanaian psychiatric hospitals, patients are beaten if they refuse treatment which often consists of local, traditional remedies or electroconvulsive therapy.

propositions.text: Applicant also cites study on mental health and discrimination in Southern Ghana supporting risk of stigmatization and loss of familial supports.
propositions.quote: The Applicant also quotes from a recent study on mental health and discrimination in Southern Ghana in support of his submission that he would be negatively affected by societal stigmatization, discrimination and the loss of familial supports.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant relies on HRW report and study showing abuses and discrimination against mentally ill in Ghana.

propositions.text: Applicant submits stigma and cruel treatment evidence was ignored; PRRA Officer relied solely on US DOS Report claiming government efforts.
propositions.quote: According to the Applicant, the documentary evidence confirms that stigma continues to affect persons living with mental health issues and that services in psychiatric hospitals constitute cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. However, the Applicant submits that this evidence was ignored and, in reliance solely on the United States Department of State Ghana 2013 Human Rights Report (“US DOS Report”), the PRRA Officer concluded that the government of Ghana was making serious efforts to change the treatment of those who suffer from mental illness.

propositions.text: Applicant argues PRRA Officer pointed to no evidence that government efforts amounted to protection; evidence supports opposite conclusion.
propositions.quote: However, the PRRA Officer pointed to no evidence that such efforts have amounted to protection for persons with mental illness in Ghana; rather, the evidence supports the opposite conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues PRRA Officer ignored evidence of stigma and cruel treatment, relying only on government efforts without proof of protection.

propositions.text: Respondent submits PRRA Officer's reference to 'serious efforts' was taken out of context and does not show wrong test applied.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the PRRA Officer’s single reference to serious efforts is taken out of context and is insufficient to ground an argument that the Officer applied the wrong test.

propositions.text: Respondent cites Barragan Gonzalez case where 'serious efforts' wording was not error as it was drawn from Federal Court of Appeal precedent.
propositions.quote: In Barragan Gonzalez v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 502 [Barragan], Justice Boswell found that the use of the words “serious efforts” was not an error since it was drawn from the Federal Court of Appeal case, Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) v Villafranca, [1992] FCJ No 1189 (FCA).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues 'serious efforts' reference was proper and cites Barragan Gonzalez supporting no error in such wording.

propositions.text: Adequate state protection requires evidence of operational protection, not just serious efforts by the state.
propositions.quote: As I have previously stated in Beri v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 854 at para 35, adequate state protection involves more than making “serious efforts” to address problems and protect citizens (De Araujo Garcia v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 79). Instead, the focus must be on what is actually happening in a country, that is, evidence of actual or operational level protection, and not on efforts that a state is endeavouring to put in place (Hercegi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 250 at para 5).

paragraphs.summary: The court states adequate state protection requires operational evidence, not just serious efforts by the state.

propositions.text: Operational adequacy of state protection is best determined by recent evidence of actual protection, not generalities about legislation or government efforts.
propositions.quote: There are also many decisions of this Court which speak to the relevance of legislation in assessing the adequacy of state protection. As stated by Justice Gagné in Molnar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 296 at para 26: [26] Needless to say that the operational adequacy of state protection is best determined in light of the most recent evidence put before the panel, rather than through generalities based on evidence emanating from state authorities about legislative and procedural measures that the government has, or has attempted to, put in place.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains operational adequacy is assessed by recent evidence of actual protection, not general legislative measures.

propositions.text: Serious efforts by the state must be viewed at operational capacity level, not only legislative stage.
propositions.quote: Similarly in Bautista v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 1187 at para 32, Justice Kelen stated that if serious efforts of the state are considered, they should be viewed at the operational capacity level and not only at the legislative stage (citing Elcock v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), (1999) 175 FTR 116 at para 15).

paragraphs.summary: The court states serious efforts must be assessed at operational capacity, not just legislative stage.

propositions.text: PRRA Officer did not explicitly state test for state protection applied.
propositions.quote: In this case the PRRA Officer did not explicitly state what test for state protection was being applied.

propositions.text: Respondent argues mere reference to 'serious efforts' does not establish wrong test was used, citing Majlat and Medina cases.
propositions.quote: And while it is true, as the Respondent submits, that mere reference to the term “serious efforts” does not establish that the wrong test was used (Majlat v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 965 at paras 35-36; Medina v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 728 at para 11),

propositions.text: Respondent's reliance on Barragan is misplaced as operational level evaluation is required, per Justice Boswell in Barragan.
propositions.quote: the Respondent’s reliance on Barragan is misplaced. There Justice Boswell stated: Although it can be an error if the RPD fails to understand that the seriousness of the state’s efforts must be evaluated at the operational level (Toriz Gilvaja v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 598 at paragraph 39, 81 Imm LR (3d) 165), the RPD cannot be faulted for couching its analysis in the words used by the Federal Court of Appeal

paragraphs.summary: Court finds PRRA Officer did not state test applied; Respondent argues 'serious efforts' reference not error but reliance on Barragan misplaced.

propositions.text: Nothing suggests PRRA Officer understood or applied operational adequacy test; decision suggests incorrect 'serious efforts' test adopted.
propositions.quote: In this case, there is nothing in the PRRA Officer’s decision to suggest that he understood that operational adequacy of state protection is the correct test for establishing state protection under ss 96 and 97 of the IRPA. Nor is there any suggestion that he applied the operational adequacy test to the evidence before him. Read as a whole, the decision suggests that the Officer incorrectly adopted a “serious efforts” test.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds PRRA Officer likely applied incorrect 'serious efforts' test, not operational adequacy test.

propositions.text: PRRA Officer quoted US DOS Report noting discrimination against disabled persons in Ghana and government efforts to change this.
propositions.quote: The PRRA Officer quoted extensively from the US DOS Report. From it, he concluded that it was clear that “discrimination against persons with disabilities continues to be a problem in Ghana”, but that “it is also clear that the government of Ghana is making serious efforts to change this”.

propositions.text: Officer noted Ghana law prohibits discrimination against persons with disabilities and government agencies address this issue.
propositions.quote: The Officer further states, “I note that the law explicitly prohibits discrimination against persons with physical, sensory, intellectual and mental disabilities”. The Officer also references the creation of “several government agencies” and the involvement of National Government Organizations to address discrimination against people with disabilities.

paragraphs.summary: PRRA Officer relied on US DOS Report noting ongoing discrimination but government efforts and legal prohibitions against disability discrimination.

propositions.text: Applicant points out US DOS Report also acknowledges inadequate enforcement and ongoing discrimination against disabled persons in Ghana.
propositions.quote: However, as the Applicant points out, the same US DOS Report, in fact the same section quoted in the PRRA Officer’s decision, acknowledges criticisms of Ghana’s implementation of its legislative schemes. For example, The constitution prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, gender, disability, language or social status; however, enforcement was generally inadequate. […] Activists supporting the rights of persons with disabilities, including Voice Ghana (a disability advocacy organization) complained of slow implementation of the law, especially the lack of legislative instruments to implement it. Despite legal protection provided in the law, discrimination against persons with disabilities in employment and inaccessibility of public buildings continued to be problems.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues US DOS Report shows inadequate enforcement and ongoing discrimination despite laws in Ghana.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted internet articles showing operational ineffectiveness of Ghana's mental health legislation and slow implementation of Mental Health Bill.
propositions.quote: The internet articles submitted by the Applicant to the PRRA Officer also contain evidence pertaining to the operational ineffectiveness of Ghanian legislation on mental health issues. In the 2014 article from Journalists for Human Rights, “Unavailable and underfunded: mental healthcare in Ghana”, the author discusses the Mental Health Bill, stating “The massive investment required for the full implementation of what is in the Bill seems unlikely in the near future”. And, in the 2011 article titled “GHANA: Mental health bill to address stigma”, the chief psychiatrist in Ghana’s national health service recognized the importance of implementation, stating “if we pass the bill and we take steps to implement it, within five years we will see a new face of mental health in Ghana”.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submitted articles showing Ghana's mental health legislation is operationally ineffective and implementation is slow.

propositions.text: Whether Officer identified and applied correct test for state protection is reviewed on correctness standard; jurisprudence mandates operational adequacy test.
propositions.quote: Whether the Officer identified and adopted the proper test for state protection is reviewed on the correctness standard (Ruano v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1023 at para 35; Koky v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 1407, at para 19). The jurisprudence has established a clear test for state protection and it is not open to the Officer to apply a different test (Ruszo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 1004 at para 22 [Ruszo]).

propositions.text: PRRA Officer failed to identify and adopt operational adequacy test; application should be granted on this ground alone.
propositions.quote: In my view, the PRRA Officer failed to identify and adopt the operational adequacy test in his state protection analysis. On this ground alone I would grant the application.

paragraphs.summary: Court states correct test for state protection is operational adequacy; PRRA Officer failed to apply it; application granted on this ground.

propositions.text: Even if correct test intended, Officer erred by accepting evidence of abuses but failing to address evidence of lack of operational adequacy.
propositions.quote: However, even if the Officer had intended to adopt the correct test, he erred in applying it by accepting evidence that demonstrated the abuses suffered in Ghana by persons with mental illness and disability, and failing to address evidence that suggested a lack of operational adequacy in the protection of the mentally ill in Ghana.

propositions.text: Standard of review for application of correct test to evidence is reasonableness.
propositions.quote: Where the question is whether the officer properly applied the correct test to the evidence on state protection before him, the standard is reasonableness (Burai v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 565 at para 34; Ruszo at para 22).

propositions.text: Officer's focus on legislative efforts led to unreasonable conclusion that Applicant would have access to state protection.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s focus on Ghana’s serious legislative efforts led to the unreasonable decision that the Applicant would have access to state protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer unreasonably applied correct test by focusing on legislative efforts and ignoring evidence of lack of operational protection.

propositions.text: No need to address Applicant's submission on PRRA Officer's failure to consider s 97(1)(b) of IRPA
propositions.quote: Given my finding above, I need not address the Applicant’s further submission that the PRRA Officer erred in failing to consider s 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Officer must assess nature or cause of risk based on case facts, citing Lemika and Ferreira cases
propositions.quote: the Officer was required to assess the nature or cause of the risk based on the facts of the case (Lemika v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 467 at paras 27-30; Ferreira v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 756 at paras 11-13).

propositions.text: Judgment grants judicial review, sets aside CIC decision, remits for redetermination by different officer
propositions.quote: 1. The application for judicial review is granted. The decision of CIC is set aside and the matter is remitted for redetermination by a different officer;

propositions.text: No question of general importance proposed or arises
propositions.quote: 2. No question of general importance is proposed by the parties and none arises;

propositions.text: No order as to costs
propositions.quote: 3. There will be no order as to costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no need to address s 97(1)(b) submission, requires risk assessment per case facts, grants judicial review, sets aside decision, remits matter, no general importance question, no costs order.
